newsitem.title: FRANCE: Balladur raps French Socialist conditions for euro.
newsitem.headline: Balladur raps French Socialist conditions for euro.

text.p: Former French prime minister Edouard Balladur said in remarks published on Sunday he hoped Spain, Italy and Portugal would be among the first to join a single European currency but it was wrong for opposition Socialists to make this a condition for the euro.

Interviewed in the Journal du Dimanche newspaper a week ahead of French parliamentary elections, Balladur, a member of the ruling centre-right, also accused the Socialists of playing with words over their calls for a new growth pact to boost jobs.

"I hope with all my heart that Italy, Spain and Portugal will be in (the single currency) but to say that if they cannot, then we won't do monetary union, is against the (Maastricht) treaty and the interests of France," he said.

Balladur, a Gaullist who led the government from 1993 until Alain Juppe was appointed on President Jacques Chirac's election in 1995, had been asked about four conditions for monetary union floated by Socialist leader Lionel Jospin during the campaign.

These are the creation of a European "economic government" as a counterweight to the independent central bank, inclusion of Spain and Italy in the first wave of members, no overvaluation of the euro against the dollar and a pact for growth and solidarity to promote jobs.

Jospin wants his proposed economic government to have greater teeth than the planned "stability council," which would amount to an informal gathering of finance ministers for countries participating in the single currency from 1999.
Balladur said the idea of giving a political dimension to the management of the euro was already part of French policy and dismissed the left's suggestion of a brand new pact as hot air.
"If we create the euro, it will be up to governments to decide what its parity should be. It is not about making a European currenncy while giving supreme power to a group of techncians," he said.
"On the stability pact, we have to reduce our deficits. The rest is words."
A former Socialist prime minister, Michel Rocard, denied Jospin's conditions threatened to derail Maastricht but defended them as a way of bolstering Europe's social responsibilities.
"The conditions we have placed on the transition to the euro follow this necessity," he told the same paper in an interview.
"Some say that for us it's all or nothing, that we are ready to break the machine if they are not met. This is absolutely false since Maastricht cannot be renegeotiated," he said.

"Instead they concern negotiations for the next two treaties -- the one ratifying the conclusions of the intergovernmental conference (on institutional changes) and the one bringing the euro into force. That is what we are insisting about."
European Union countries are due to decide in May 1998 which countries can join the euro by studying economic data for 1997.
The first stage of France's two-round parliamentary is on May 25, followed by a run-off on June 1.
The last opinion polls published before a ban came into force on Sunday suggested Juppe's centre-right coalition would stay in government but with a reduced majority.
